metadata.title: FCE Gap-Fill - 12 Gaps
metadata.description: Open cloze with gap 0 as example. Gaps test grammar across the sentence: auxiliaries, passive, modals, conditionals, reported speech, relatives, linking words, gerunds and infinitives, phrasal verbs, fixed expressions, dependent prepositions, plus the determiners and comparisons the exam also tests. 'area' on each gap names it; a slash lists accepted alternatives.

exercises.title: The Dog on the Bus

exercises.title: The Cloud Society
exercises.text:

exercises.title: The Bookshop Cat
exercises.text:

exercises.title: The Puppet Maker
exercises.text:

exercises.title: The Village Sign
exercises.text:

Many argued that the mistake {{5}} now become part of local history, and that changing it would be {{6}} pointless as it was expensive. {{7}} only that, but the misspelt sign had suddenly become famous. exercises.title: The Winter Bird Count
exercises.text:

The rules are simple. Participants choose an hour and write {{3}} every bird that lands in their garden or local park. They record the highest number of each species seen at any {{4}} time, so no blackbird is counted twice. The information {{5}} then sent to scientists, who use it to track changes in bird populations.

The results can be surprising. Some once-common species have become much {{6}} frequent visitors, while others now appear in greater numbers than they used to.

exercises.title: Beating Stage Fright
exercises.text:
If the thought of speaking in front of an audience makes your hands shake, you are certainly not the {{0}} one. Many people fear it even {{1}} than spiders. The good news is that, with a little practice, almost anyone can learn to cope {{2}} it.

Firstly, accept that nerves are normal. Even experienced actors and presenters feel anxious before they perform. Rather {{3}} trying to get rid of these feelings completely, see them as a sign that your body is getting ready.

Secondly, prepare thoroughly. Many speakers {{4}} the mistake {{5}} learning their speech word for word. {{6}} they forget a single line, they panic. It is much better to know your main points well, {{7}} that you can speak naturally.

Thirdly, don't rush. Nervous speakers tend to talk far too quickly, which makes them hard to follow.

Finally, remember that most audiences want you to succeed. {{8}} from waiting for you to fail, they are usually on your side from the moment you begin. You {{9}} try to make eye contact with a few friendly faces.

Above {{10}}, keep going. {{11}} matter how badly your first attempt goes, {{12}} talk you give makes the next one a little easier.

exercises.title: Message in a Bottle
exercises.text:
When eleven-year-old Isla Grant went for a walk on a Cornish beach last March, the last thing she expected to find was {{0}} message from the past. Half buried in the sand was {{1}} bottle {{2}} a note inside. 'At first I thought it was just rubbish,' she says. 'I almost walked straight {{3}} it.'

Isla was determined to track Pierre {{8}}. She posted a photo of the note online, and {{9}} than two days later, she received a reply. Pierre {{10}} thrown the bottle into the sea while on holiday and had completely forgotten {{11}} it. 'I can't believe it survived all that time,' he wrote. It had probably drifted around the Atlantic for years before finally washing up in Cornwall.

The two have been writing to each other ever since. Isla, meanwhile, is planning to send a bottle of her own. 'I just hope someone finds it before I'm {{12}} old as Pierre,' she laughs.

exercises.title: Never Too Old to Skate
exercises.text:

exercises.title: The Art of Queuing
exercises.text:
If there is one thing the British are famous {{0}}, it is queuing. Visitors are amazed to see people queuing patiently at bus stops, even if there are only two of them.

But queuing has not always been a national habit. {{1}} to some historians, it became common in the nineteenth century, when people moved to the cities in large numbers. During the Second World War, when food was scarce, people often {{2}} to wait for hours {{3}} end.

Today, the unwritten rules are surprisingly strict. You must never push in, and you {{4}} leave a polite amount of space {{5}} yourself and the person in front. If someone does jump the queue, few people will say anything directly. Instead, they sigh loudly or mutter to themselves. This, it seems, {{6}} considered far more acceptable than actually complaining.

Not everyone sees queuing {{7}} a good thing, of course. {{8}} average person spends {{9}} to six months of their life waiting in line. Still, most agree that queuing is fair: {{10}} arrives first is served first, no matter who they are. Some even enjoy it. 'It's the only place where strangers actually talk to you,' says one pensioner. 'I've {{11}} more friends at the post office {{12}} I ever made at work.'
